No. The story is told in a conventional, linear way: close third-person on Nora, in chronological order across four section breaks (night wandering, nursery, morning discharge, home).

It does use a revelation (the baby switch) and an open-ended ending, but both are handled within a standard literary-realist arc. The structure is not fragmented, and it uses no unusual format, shifting perspectives, genre blending or typographic play. Its strengths are in language, imagery and emotional subtlety rather than inventive form. The pinwheel hospital and the dreamlike, disorienting night are thematic and atmospheric touches, not structural experiments.
